page.title: Ship Equipment Salvaging
page.t: Recover installed equipment from eligible ships for later reuse.

A black-market hand-laser regulator associated with Riptide scrap crews and Avarice chop-shop operators. It forces a standard hand laser into a tighter, unstable cutting arc capable of slicing damaged hull plating, equipment mounts, and exposed component housings. Illegal in most regulated sectors due to its use in unauthorized salvage, equipment theft, and shipboard tampering.
Illegal black-market hand-laser regulator that drives a tight, unstable cutting arc for unauthorized salvage and equipment recovery.

A black-market hand-laser regulator developed from the same improvised principles as the Avarice Beam Regulator. It reshapes the beam into a crude welding arc for fastening salvaged equipment back onto compatible ship frames. Illegal in most civilized sectors due to unauthorized ship modification, unsafe field repairs, and unregistered equipment installs.
Illegal black-market hand-laser regulator that reshapes the beam into a crude welding arc for fitting salvaged equipment to compatible ship frames.

A disposable black-market focusing insert for the Avarice Beam Regulator. It briefly stabilizes a hand laser's cutting arc beyond licensed civilian limits, allowing ship equipment to be separated from its mount without destroying the part outright. Illegal in most regulated sectors due to its association with equipment theft and unauthorized salvage.

A disposable black-market field-welding compound for the Avarice Bonding Regulator. When excited by the regulator, it forms a temporary conductive lattice between a salvaged component and a compatible ship mount. Illegal in most regulated sectors due to unlicensed ship modification and field installation of salvaged equipment.

GalNet - Shipyards Warn Against Unlicensed Salvage Crews

Across the known systems, shipyard operators are reporting a sharp increase in unauthorized salvage work around repair berths, construction queues, and abandoned holding yards.

The incidents appear to follow a similar pattern. Small EVA crews approach disabled or ownerless ships, use compact cutting beams to free valuable components, and depart before yard security can establish ownership, liability, or even a repair ticket. In several reported cases, technicians claim the same crews later returned with bonding rigs to refit recovered parts onto privately owned vessels.

Mora Tilen, a spokesperson for an independent shipyard consortium, spoke to GalNet about the growing concern.

"This is not salvage in any responsible sense. It is unlicensed shipbuilding in a pressure suit. These crews are bypassing certification, warranty records, safety checks, and every fee that keeps a yard operational. The fact that some of them appear unusually well supplied only makes the matter more troubling."

Port authorities have stopped short of naming a single supplier, but several investigations now point to anonymous dockside dealers moving compact industrial tools and volatile field catalysts through black-market channels. Yard officials insist this trade is limited and dangerous. Independent captains, predictably, are less convinced.

GalNet can only note that the argument is unlikely to fade while damaged hulls continue to outnumber available repair crews. For pilots willing to trust a dealer over a dockmaster, the warning may read less like a prohibition and more like a shopping list.

Ralen Voss
Industrial Affairs Correspondent, GalNet
GalNet - Unregistered Ship Components Surface in Dockside Trade

Authorities across several major trade corridors are investigating a sudden rise in unregistered ship components appearing in private dockside sales. Unlike ordinary scrap, the seized goods include intact drive assemblies, shield cores, weapon housings, and turret interfaces carrying serial records from ships reported abandoned, dismantled, or missing from licensed repair queues.

Shipyard representatives insist that legitimate yards are not responsible for the new supply. Several affected operators claim their inventories remain balanced, while independent repair crews report being approached by brokers offering complete components with no installation history and no questions attached.

A Teladi trade assessor, speaking to GalNet on condition of anonymity, described the development as an inevitable correction.

"Pilots have always paid for convenience. The only difference is that someone has finally worked out how to put convenience in a crate and move it through the back door."

Port authorities have issued a general advisory warning captains that equipment purchased outside an accredited yard may carry altered identifiers, voided warranties, or links to unresolved salvage claims. Nevertheless, reports indicate that Black Market contacts are already circulating revised stock lists, with availability varying sharply from one station to the next. Higher-grade components remain scarce, but investigators expect the supply to change as quickly as damaged ships disappear from contested sectors.

For licensed shipyards, this is evidence of an expanding criminal supply chain. For independent captains, it may simply mean that a familiar contact now has something more substantial hidden behind the counter.

Ralen Voss
Industrial Affairs Correspondent, GalNet

A turret-mounted salvage beam built by Riptide scrap crews on an integrated mining-turret frame for M-class ships, tuned with the same regulator principle as the handheld Avarice Beam Regulator. It tracks and cuts unclaimed small and medium wrecks on its own. Only Riptide salvage lasers and turrets can harvest wrecks; ordinary mining turrets cannot. Requires a Riptide Salvage Laser or Riptide Salvage Turret.

A forward-mounted salvage beam built by Riptide scrap crews on a mining-laser frame, tuned with the same regulator principle as the handheld Avarice Beam Regulator. Its cutting arc separates plating, housings and intact parts from unclaimed small and medium wrecks. Only Riptide salvage lasers and turrets can harvest wrecks; ordinary mining lasers cannot. Requires a Riptide Salvage Laser or Riptide Salvage Turret.
